definition.text: Complementary goods are goods used together, so that one becomes more attractive as the other becomes more popular.

facts.text: Demand for a complement rises when the price of the other good falls, giving a negative cross elasticity of demand.
Cars and petrol, phones and phone service, and printers and cartridges are examples.
Razors have been sold cheaply as loss leaders to raise demand for the blades.
A perfect complement must be consumed with the other good, like left and right shoes; its indifference curve forms a right angle.
Complementarity need not be mutual: a game needs a console, but a console does not need that game.

definition.text: Substitute goods are goods that can replace each other, so cheaper prices for one reduce demand for the other.

facts.text: Two products with a positive cross elasticity of demand are substitutes.
A perfect substitute can be used in exactly the same way as the good it replaces, and its indifference curves are straight lines.
Someone who sees Coca-Cola and Pepsi Max as perfect substitutes would be happy spending the whole budget on either one.
As a consumer accumulates more of one good, they will pay less for each extra unit of its substitute.

definition.text: Consumer choice theory is the part of microeconomics that explains how people's preferences shape what they spend and how much they demand.

facts.text: It assumes consumers maximise utility subject to their budget constraint, choosing the best bundle they can afford.
Preferences are drawn as indifference curves, each showing bundles that leave the consumer equally satisfied.
Income, culture, product information and psychological factors all affect how consumers value goods.
Every price change splits into an income effect and a substitution effect.
Behavioural economists criticise the theory because consumers often rely on heuristics, rough shortcuts that ignore some information.
People often let sunk costs sway them, like travelling through a storm to use a concert ticket.

definition.text: The income effect is the change in how much of a good people buy when their real income, or purchasing power, changes.

facts.text: With prices fixed, a change in income shifts the budget line in parallel: outward when income rises, inward when it falls.
A good bought more as income rises is a normal good; one bought less is an inferior good.
Together with the substitution effect, it makes up the full effect of a price change.

definition.text: Economists have offered many definitions of their subject, from the study of wealth to the study of choices under scarcity.

facts.text: Economics was first called political economy, stretching the Greek idea of household management to the running of a state.
In 1803 Jean-Baptiste Say defined it as the science of producing, distributing and consuming wealth.
Alfred Marshall in 1890 called it the study of mankind in the ordinary business of life, tied to the material requisites of well-being.
Lionel Robbins in 1932 defined it as the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means with alternative uses, perhaps the most commonly accepted definition today.
